introduction: These readings warn. Bahá’u’lláh tells the peoples of the world that an unforeseen calamity follows them; ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, in Europe and America before 1914, says that a universal war is coming, and afterwards that a fiercer one will follow unless its causes are removed. The readings describe the wars of their time, trace them to the neglect of divine counsel and to prejudice and greed, comfort those caught in the turmoil, and look beyond it to an old order rolled up and a new one spread out. The Hebrew prophets, the Gospels’ discourse on the last days and the Qur’an speak in the same register, and poets from Tennyson to Yeats and Owen saw the same wars. Other voices check an easy reading: Jesus on the tower of Siloam and Voltaire on Lisbon deny that the victims of a calamity are its guilty, Jonah and Jeremiah show that a warning can be answered, and Crane and the Preacher doubt that disaster carries any meaning at all.
questions: The readings trace wars and calamities to disobedience of divine counsel. Jesus said those crushed by the tower of Siloam were no worse than others. How can both be held without blaming those who suffer?
Nineveh repented and was spared. What in these readings shows that the warnings are appeals and not fixed forecasts?
William James admitted that war attracts because it is the strong life. What in the readings offers people a harder and better use of the same energies?
The readings say the old order will be rolled up and a new one spread out; Burke feared what is lost when an order is replaced. What should be carried across?
Several readings comfort people who were living through war. Which words would you take to someone in such a place today?
Yeats, Arnold and Hardy saw the same breakdown and drew little hope from it. What grounds for hope do the readings give that the poets lacked?

outside.why: Paul warned in the same terms that the day comes as a thief in the night, when people are saying peace and safety.
Lamentations begins with the same sight: how doth the city sit solitary that was full of people.
Isaiah's vision of peace is of the gains that follow it: swords beaten into ploughshares, and war learned no more.
Jesus called the peacemakers blessed, and said they shall be called the children of God.
Hosea said of his own nation that the people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.
Tennyson in 1842 foresaw the nations' airy navies grappling in the central blue, and a rain of ghastly dew.
A general who became president counted the cost of armament differently: every gun made is a theft from those who hunger. Does the intolerable cost of weapons end war, or only change who pays for it?
Tennyson's dying king says that the old order changes, yielding place to new, lest one good custom corrupt the world.
Kant defined enlightenment as the courage to use one's own understanding and leave inherited tutelage behind.
John's Gospel says that light came into the world and people loved darkness rather than light.
Thomas Hardy, months before the Great War, had God remark that the nations were striving to make red war yet redder.
James asks where wars and fightings come from, and answers: from the desires that war within you.
Yeats wrote after the Great War that things fall apart and the centre cannot hold.
Luke's Gospel speaks of distress of nations with perplexity, and hearts failing for fear of what is coming.
Ezekiel says that the watchman who sees the sword coming and blows the trumpet has done his part, whatever the people do.
Amos explains why a prophet speaks in public: the lion has roared, who will not fear?
Jesus wept over Jerusalem because it did not know the things that belonged to its peace.
The Qur’an says that corruption appears on land and sea because of what human hands have done.

Jesus denied that the eighteen on whom the tower fell were worse sinners than their neighbours. How should a reader speak of calamity as the result of disobedience without blaming those who suffer it?
The Gospel tells its readers that they will hear of wars and rumours of wars, and that the end is not yet.

Kant thought that lasting peace needs a federation of free states and that laws lose force as an empire widens. What kind of agreement among nations would prevent the fiercer war this reading foresees?
Jeremiah charged the leaders of his day with healing the hurt of the people slightly, saying peace when there was no peace.
Lincoln said of a nation divided over slavery that a house divided against itself cannot stand.
The Gospel speaks of a tribulation greater than any since the beginning of the world, shortened for the elect's sake.
Shelley's traveller finds the wreck of a king's statue, and around it the lone and level sands.

Marx saw the same restlessness and gave it another cause: under the rule of capital all that is solid melts into air. Is the instability of political orders a spiritual matter or an economic one, or can it be both?
Isaiah saw the earth reel to and fro like a drunkard under the weight of its transgression.
Isaiah described his nation as a body: the whole head sick and the whole heart faint.
Shakespeare's king states the surgeon's rule: diseases desperate grown are by desperate appliance relieved, or not at all.
Abraham asked whether the Judge of all the earth would destroy the righteous with the wicked. What may a believer say to God about the cost of a severe remedy?
Paul uses the same picture of a body whose members cannot say to one another, I have no need of thee.
Isaiah says that truth is fallen in the street and equity cannot enter.
Hosea's line for such a time: they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.
Wordsworth saw the same race in his own day: getting and spending, we lay waste our powers.
Jeremiah hears the trumpet and the alarm of war: destruction upon destruction is cried.
Hobbes held both sayings true: man is a god to man, and man is a wolf to man. Which conditions bring out the one, and which the other?
The Gospel calls nation rising against nation the beginning of sorrows, the first pains of a birth.

Dickens opened his novel of revolution by remarking that every age thinks itself the best and the worst of times. How would one tell whether the present turmoil is different from the turmoil of other ages?
Hardy stood in a frozen landscape at the century's end and heard a thrush sing of some hope he could not see. Where does hope come from when the evidence gives so little cause?
The psalm says that God is our refuge though the earth be removed and the mountains carried into the sea.
Thucydides has the Athenians say that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
The Book of Revelation has an angel cry over a great trading city: Babylon the great is fallen.
Kipling warned the British Empire at its height that its navies melt away and its pomp is one with Nineveh and Tyre.
The seer of Revelation saw a pale horse whose rider was Death, with power to kill by sword and hunger.
Mark Twain wrote out what a prayer for victory silently asks for: the ruin of other people's homes.
Wilfred Owen asked what passing-bells there are for those who die as cattle, and answered: only the monstrous anger of the guns.
Joel has the nations summoned to beat their ploughshares into swords. Why do scriptures that long for peace also speak in the voice of war?

Lincoln, in the midst of civil war, thought it might be God's will that every drop of blood drawn by the lash be paid by another drawn by the sword. Can a war be read as a judgment without being called good?
The Dhammapada observes that victory breeds hatred, for the conquered lie down in sorrow.

William James, a pacifist, admitted that showing war's horror has no effect, since for many war is the strong life, and looked for a moral equivalent. What can give a people the hardiness they seek in war?
Shakespeare's king calls his men to imitate the tiger and stiffen the sinews. Why has war so often been praised as the school of character, and what answers that praise?
David's lament for Saul and Jonathan has given every age its words: how are the mighty fallen.
Shakespeare's king observes that sorrows come not as single spies but in battalions.
Jesus told his friends that in the world they would have tribulation, and to be of good cheer.
Habakkuk resolved that though the fields should yield no food, yet he would rejoice in the Lord.
Isaiah counsels his people to enter their chambers and hide for a little moment, until the indignation is past.
The psalm promises that one need not fear the terror by night nor the destruction that wastes at noonday.
The Qur’an warns of a chastisement that does not fall only on those who do wrong. What follows for the innocent when a whole people is caught in calamity?
Matthew Arnold heard the sea of faith withdrawing down the shingles of the world.
The Qur’an says that it is not the eyes that grow blind but the hearts.
Arnold described himself as wandering between two worlds, one dead, the other powerless to be born. What is it like to live faithfully in the interval?
Hosea says that the nation saw its sickness and sent to a foreign king, who could not heal it.
The Qur’an pictures unbelief as darkness upon darkness on a vast abysmal sea.
Amos holds that the Lord does nothing without revealing His counsel to His servants the prophets.
Proverbs gives the old rule: train up a child in the way he should go.
Jesus said it would be as in the days of Noah: they ate, they drank, they married, until the flood came.
After the Lisbon earthquake Voltaire asked whether there was more vice in fallen Lisbon than in Paris. Is every calamity a retribution, and for whose deeds?
Paul says that the whole creation groans and travails in pain together until now.
Zephaniah announces a day of wrath, of trouble and distress, of darkness and gloominess.
Joel asks of the great and terrible day: who can abide it?
Amos warned those who looked forward to the day of the Lord that it would be darkness and not light for them. Who should be most sobered by passages like this one?
Ezekiel is told to speak whether the people will hear or whether they will forbear.
The first letter of Peter tells its readers not to think the fiery trial a strange thing.
The second psalm asks why the nations rage and the peoples imagine a vain thing.
In the parable the wheat and the tares grow together until the harvest, and are then separated.
Ezekiel is told to call the breath from the four winds to breathe upon the slain.
Haggai hears the Lord say that He will shake the heavens, the earth and all nations.
Isaiah hears the promise of new heavens and a new earth, in which the former shall not be remembered.
The seer of Revelation saw a new heaven and a new earth, the first having passed away.
Burke held that a state must be able to change in order to be conserved, and distrusted those who would roll up an order all at once. What is lost when an order is replaced rather than reformed?
The psalm that speaks of desolations ends with the command: be still, and know that I am God.
Paul speaks of things that eye has not seen nor ear heard, prepared for those who love God.
The Preacher saw that the battle is not to the strong, and that time and chance happen to all. How much of what historians record is wisdom at work, and how much is chance?
Paul ends his own account of history's turns by calling God's judgments unsearchable.
Stephen Crane's man tells the universe that he exists, and the universe replies that this creates no sense of obligation. What would persuade someone of that mind that a disaster holds any wisdom?
Paul wrote from prison that what had happened to him had served to advance the message.
The psalm says that weeping may endure for a night, but joy comes in the morning.
Isaiah says that the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.
Zechariah's song speaks of a dayspring that gives light to those who sit in darkness and guides them into peace.
The Qur’an says that God is able to divide a people into parties and make them taste the violence of one another.
Tennyson looked beyond the wars he foresaw to a time when the battle-flags are furled in the parliament of man.
The Qur’an speaks of a day when the earth is shaken and yields up her burdens, and man asks what ails her.
Jesus said that he came not to send peace but a sword, and that households would be divided over him.
When Nineveh turned from its evil way, God did not do what He had said He would do. Is a warning of retribution a prediction, or an appeal that may still be answered?
Jeremiah says that if a nation turns from its evil, God will repent of the evil He thought to do to it. How firmly should anyone hold to a forecast of how many will perish?
The founders of UNESCO wrote that since wars begin in the minds of men, it is there that the defences of peace must be built.
The Letter to the Hebrews reads suffering as discipline: whom the Lord loves He chastens.
Shelley ends his ode to the destroying wind with a question that is also a hope: if winter comes, can spring be far behind?
Yeats, watching his world come apart, asked what rough beast was slouching toward Bethlehem to be born.
Daniel foresaw kingdoms broken in pieces and a kingdom set up that shall never be destroyed.

psalm-refuge-and-strength.text: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea; Though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with the swelling thereof

isaiah-earth-shall-reel.text: The earth is utterly broken down, the earth is clean dissolved, the earth is moved exceedingly. The earth shall reel to and fro like a drunkard, and shall be removed like a cottage; and the transgression thereof shall be heavy upon it; and it shall fall, and not rise again

joel-plowshares-into-swords.text: Proclaim ye this among the Gentiles; Prepare war, wake up the mighty men, let all the men of war draw near; let them come up: Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruninghooks into spears: let the weak say, I am strong

luke-distress-of-nations.text: And there shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars; and upon the earth distress of nations, with perplexity; the sea and the waves roaring; Men's hearts failing them for fear, and for looking after those things which are coming on the earth: for the powers of heaven shall be shaken

matthew-great-tribulation.text: For then shall be great tribulation, such as was not since the beginning of the world to this time, no, nor ever shall be. And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened

revelation-pale-horse.text: And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him. And power was given unto them over the fourth part of the earth, to kill with sword, and with hunger, and with death, and with the beasts of the earth

revelation-babylon-is-fallen.text: And he cried mightily with a strong voice, saying, Babylon the great is fallen

jeremiah-destruction-upon-destruction.text: My bowels, my bowels! I am pained at my very heart; my heart maketh a noise in me; I cannot hold my peace, because thou hast heard, O my soul, the sound of the trumpet, the alarm of war. Destruction upon destruction is cried; for the whole land is spoiled: suddenly are my tents spoiled, and my curtains in a moment

isaiah-until-the-indignation-be-overpast.text: Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast

genesis-grieved-him-at-his-heart.text: And God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. And it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart

jonah-god-repented.text: And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not

isaiah-make-his-paths-straight.text: The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain

matthew-beginning-of-sorrows.text: For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places. All these are the beginning of sorrows

jeremiah-evil-shall-go-forth.text: Thus saith the Lord of hosts, Behold, evil shall go forth from nation to nation, and a great whirlwind shall be raised up from the coasts of the earth

isaiah-nations-as-a-drop.text: Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing

daniel-time-of-trouble.text: And at that time shall Michael stand up, the great prince which standeth for the children of thy people: and there shall be a time of trouble, such as never was since there was a nation even to that same time: and at that time thy people shall be delivered, every one that shall be found written in the book

quran-trial-not-on-wrongdoers-only.text: And guard yourselves against a chastisement which cannot fall exclusively on those of you who are wrong-doers, and know that Allah is severe in punishment.

quran-earth-is-shaken.text: When Earth is shaken with her (final) earthquake And Earth yieldeth up her burdens, And man saith: What aileth her? That day she will relate her chronicles, Because thy Lord inspireth her

quran-taste-the-violence.text: Say: He is able to send punishment upon you from above you or from beneath your feet, or to bewilder you with dissension and make you taste the tyranny one of another. See how We display the revelations so that they may understand.

quran-would-not-destroy-the-townships.text: In truth thy Lord destroyed not the townships tyrannously while their folk were doing right.

quran-quake-of-the-hour.text: O mankind! Fear your Lord. Lo! the earthquake of the Hour (of Doom) is a tremendous thing.

hardy-red-war-yet-redder.text: The world is as it used to be: / 'And all nations striving strong to make / Red war yet redder
hardy-red-war-yet-redder.author: Thomas Hardy

james-war-is-the-strong-life.text: Showing war's irrationality and horror is of no effect upon him. The horrors make the fascination. War is the strong life; it is life in extremis
james-war-is-the-strong-life.author: William James
